notes: Coaching path: PRD built section by section with batched writes

turns.text:
Brain dump. Product: "Ledgerleaf" — a small, privacy-first household budgeting app for couples who share some expenses and keep others separate. Today they use a shared spreadsheet that one partner maintains and the other never opens, or a bank-linked app that exposes everything to both of them and sells their data. What's broken: no clean concept of "mine / yours / ours" money, month-end reconciliation is a fight, and nobody trusts aggregator apps with bank credentials.

Who: two-person households, 25-45, both employed, at least one irregular income source (freelance, tips, commission). Primary persona is the "spreadsheet keeper" who resents being the household accountant; secondary is the partner who wants a 10-second answer to "can we afford this".

What I know I want: manual and CSV/OFX import only (no bank credential aggregation, ever); three ledgers per household (mine, yours, ours) with explicit transfers between them; a monthly "settle up" that computes who owes whom for shared categories using a configurable split (50/50, proportional to income, custom per category); envelope-style budgets with rollover; a "can we afford it" quick check that answers from remaining envelope balance; local-first storage with end-to-end encrypted sync between the two partners' devices; export everything to CSV at any time.

Out of scope for v1: bank linking, investments, net-worth tracking, bill pay, kids/allowance, more than two adults, tax prep. Not sure: receipts OCR — maybe later.

Business: solo founder, subscription of a few dollars a month, success = 1,000 paying households in 12 months with 6-month retention above 60%. Stakes: side project that I want to be taken seriously — internal-quality is too low, but it's not an enterprise launch.

Anything else? No, that's it. Let's do the Coaching path please, and use the Vision + Features entry point. Skip web research for this one, I know the space.

Concern scan: all good, you nailed it. Add one: "settle-up history" — an audit of past months so nobody argues about what was agreed. Agree with the exclusions.

Form factor: phone-first, native iOS and Android, each partner on their own phone. Yes, the keeper does need a bigger screen for CSV import and month-end settle-up, so a lightweight web app on desktop for import and settle-up only is in v1. The web app uses the same E2E-encrypted data, keys never leave the devices.

Vision:
1. Pitch: "Your money, your partner's money, and the money you share — finally three separate piles, with the month-end argument done for you in one tap, and no bank password ever leaving your phone."
2. Six months in: nobody is the household accountant anymore. The partner who never opened the spreadsheet checks "can we afford it" before big purchases. Month-end settle-up takes five minutes and ends with a transfer, not a fight. Both feel their personal spending is private-ish, not surveilled.
3. Why it deserves to exist: the spreadsheet can't do mine/yours/ours or settle-up and one person always owns it; aggregator apps want your bank credentials and monetise your data. Worth it for couples who value privacy and fairness over zero-effort. Obviously not for people who want automatic categorisation of everything, or solo budgeters, or anyone who wants net-worth dashboards.

Vision reads right, keep "by construction, not by policy". Glossary is fine.

Private-ish, decided: personal ledgers are private by default at the transaction level. Sam opening Alex's personal ledger sees nothing except one line: the balance bucket total is hidden too. What the partner CAN see from a personal ledger is only what the owner explicitly shares: a transaction becomes visible when it is tagged as shared or when it is the funding side of a shared expense (e.g. Alex paid a shared grocery bill from personal money, so that single transaction shows up in settle-up with merchant, amount and date, nothing else about the personal ledger).

Incomes: Sam sees the split ratio and the resulting percentages ("58/42") but never the underlying income numbers. Each partner enters their own income, the app stores it encrypted and only the ratio is derived and shared.

Settle-up shows its work: every shared-category transaction with who paid, plus the funded-from-personal transactions as described above. That is the one place the boundary opens, deliberately, and the app says so in plain words on the settle-up screen.

Ratio leak: good catch. Decision: reword the promise honestly. Couples who opt into income-proportional splitting have had that conversation, so the product says "the split ratio reveals the relative incomes", and also offers the 50/50 and custom-per-category splits that reveal nothing. Resolve the open question that way.

Feature grouping: approved as is, including 5.2 and 5.6 as separate features. Start with 5.1 then 5.5, then the rest, in your order.

5.1: Alex opens Ledgerleaf, taps the quick-add button, enters 62.00 and the merchant. The app proposes the last-used ledger. Alex taps "split this purchase", enters 40.00 as shared groceries (ours ledger, Groceries category) and the remaining 22.00 stays in Alex's personal ledger as Personal. The card payment is recorded once, paid from Alex's personal account, so the shared part appears in settle-up as "Alex paid 40.00 for Ours" and that is the funding-side exception we already agreed. Whole thing under 15 seconds, one hand, no confirmation dialog, an undo toast for 10 seconds.

Transfers: people move money between ledgers to fund shared envelopes at the start of the month or to reimburse. The app asks for amount, from-ledger, to-ledger and an optional note, nothing else. Transfers are never edited, only reversed by a new opposite transfer, which keeps the history honest.

Categories: we ship a starter set (about 15), each household can rename, add and archive. One category set per household shared across all three ledgers, so reports line up; personal ledgers can hide categories from their own view but not from the set.

Entry and Payer: keep the names.

Gap 1 (correcting an Entry): the personal/frozen distinction is right. An Entry that touches only a personal ledger and has not reached a settlement can be edited in place by its owner; the edit is itself recorded in an edit history visible to the owner only. Any Entry with a share in Ours is editable only until the month is settled, and an edit to the shared part is visible to the partner as "edited" with the previous amount. After settlement it is frozen and can only be corrected by a reversing adjustment in the next period.

Gap 2 (tag as shared later): yes, that route exists but it is for retroactive catch-up, e.g. imported statement rows. Marking a personal transaction as shared splits off nothing: the whole amount moves into Ours with the owner as Payer, and the partner is notified. Sam can decline within the open period, which sends it back to personal.

5.5 settle-up on 1 November: either partner can start the close on the 1st or later. The app shows October's shared spending: each transaction, who paid, the split rule applied, the funded-from-personal ones marked, and one number at the bottom: "Alex owes Sam 137.00". The initiator taps Propose. The other partner gets a notification, reviews the same list, and taps Accept. When both have accepted the settlement is sealed: immutable, stored in Settlement History with a hash of its contents. The app does not move money; it says who owes whom and offers to record the transfer between ledgers once they have paid each other outside the app. The settlement closes on both accepts, not on payment; the payment is recorded as a Transfer when it happens.

Disagreement: no dispute mechanism in v1. Sam taps any line, "ask about this", which sends a note to the other partner attached to that transaction. Then whoever entered it edits it, since the period is still open; the proposal is withdrawn and re-proposed automatically when anything changes. Acceptance is always of the exact list on screen.

Late transaction: a receipt dated 28 October entered on 3 November goes into November, flagged "dated October", and shows up in November's settle-up. Settled months are never reopened.

Your reasoning for separating close from payment is mine too. Philosophy line stays.

Answers on the 5.5 edges so you can close them: (a) stall: a proposal that sits for 7 days gets one reminder to the other partner, then a second at 14 days; it never auto-accepts and never expires, October stays open and visibly "waiting on Alex". (b) periods must seal in order, oldest first; if October is unsealed, November can still be used and entered, but cannot be proposed until October is sealed. A partner can instead "carry forward" an unsealed month to the next one: both accept, it merges into a combined two-month settlement. (c) re-propose only on material changes (amount, payer, split, category of a shared line); a quiet window batches notifications to one a day.

5.2 pairing: Sam installs, creates the household, pays (one subscription per household, billed to Sam via the app store; if Sam stops paying the household goes read-only for both after a 30 day grace period, data stays exportable). Sam taps "invite partner" which shows a QR code and a one-time link valid for 24 hours. Alex installs the app, scans the QR in person, or opens the link; the key exchange happens device-to-device, and Alex sets their own passcode/biometrics. Alex must confirm a short verification code that matches on both phones, otherwise nobody joins. Cold start: Sam can use the app fully solo, entering and importing a month of transactions; they sync to Alex when Alex joins, but personal ledger of Sam stays private from the first day. Alex is useful as soon as they have joined: they see Ours and their own empty personal ledger, and the first thing they are asked is to enter their income for the split. Browser: Sam goes to the web address, the page shows a QR code, Sam scans it with the phone app (Settings, Authorise a browser), the phone sends the keys encrypted to the browser session. Per session, expires after 12 hours idle or on closing the tab, and the phone can revoke it any time. Alex can authorise their own browser the same way; each partner's browser only sees what that partner can see.

5.2 gaps. Lapsed card: you're right, fix it: a lapsed household stays read-only for shared data (Ours, settlements) but each partner keeps writing their own personal ledger and can export everything. Household ends: v1 non-goal, written down as an explicit choice: a household can be dissolved by either partner alone, which revokes the other's access to shared data going forward, stops sync of Ours to the leaver, and lets each partner export Ours and their own ledger as CSV; sealed settlements stay in each partner's exported history. No splitting-of-assets features. The safety surface matters: one partner can leave unilaterally and immediately; the other partner is told only that the household was dissolved, no reason, no location data anywhere in the product.

5.3 budgeting: on the 1st Sam opens "This month", sees the envelope list (category, planned amount, rolled-over amount, spent, left). Envelopes exist only for Ours and for each partner's own personal ledger (private to the owner); the one-tap "copy last month" is the main way to set up. Irregular income: Ledgerleaf budgets against a conservative floor that the household sets (default the lowest of the last six months of income, entered by each partner); income above the floor lands in an "unallocated" pool that gets assigned when money arrives, never earlier. Nothing is promised to an envelope until the money exists. Rollover: any envelope can roll over or reset to zero, chosen per envelope. A shared envelope that rolls over keeps its balance in Ours, owned by the household; it is not attributed to either partner at settle-up, because settle-up only compares what each partner paid against their share of spending, not balances.

To save time, for 5.4 (Statement Import), 5.6 (Can We Afford It) and 5.7 (Data Ownership and Recovery) please draft them yourself in one batch from everything I've told you, with [ASSUMPTION] tags where you inferred. I'll react to the drafts. Then carry on to the remaining sections the same way.

Assumptions: 1. Accept, but allow a second device per partner in v1 (phone plus tablet or a second phone) as the mitigation; export reminders as the fallback. 2. Keep your no-verdict design, I like it. 3. Import is desktop web only in v1, agreed. 4. Importer's personal ledger by default, agreed. Floor: either partner can change their own income, the floor is derived from both and needs both to accept a change to the method.

No number for partner-#2 activation, please draft a candidate with a counter-metric for me to shoot at.

Go ahead with the whole next batch in one pass, then straight into Finalize including the reviewer gate: run all reviewers in parallel and apply what they raise. I'll answer any real decisions at the end.

1. Yes to both: Transfers into Ours count as contributions; unspent residue in Ours is owed to neither partner and split by the default rule. 2. Stall: a proposal that sits unanswered for 30 days can be closed one-sidedly by the proposer; it is sealed as "closed without acceptance" in Settlement History, visibly different, and the other partner can attach a dissent note. 3. Opt-in client-side aggregate telemetry: off by default, asked once, counts only (no ledger content, no amounts), a plain-words explanation, and a switch to turn it off. Add it as an FR and to MVP. 4. Ratified, keep the Contribution Floor. 5. Yes, dissolution must not leak timing: the remaining partner is told only on their next app open, showing the date only. 6. Acquisition: not a PRD concern for v1, record it as an open question for go-to-market. Fold all of this in and close the PRD out as final.
